column2: No contracts have been entered into with lending institutions with a view to constructing rental housing projects. Details of the projects have not been submitted nor approved, nor have any guarantees been made to the lending institutions concerned with respect to return on their investment.

column1: The corporation has also approved the investment of one lending institution in Toronto in acquiring land and erecting a six unit rental project. However, in this case the corporation has given no guarantee to the lending institution concerned with respect to return on the investment.
Approval of these investments has been given in accordance with section II (subsection 9) of the National Housing Act, 1944.

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,LEGISLATIVE PROGRAMME-PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS-WEDNESDAY EVENING SITTINGS,,"Mr. Speaker, before this motion is made, may I have the permission of the house and of Your Honour to make a statement respecting the business of the house.

My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked on Monday if I would give the house a statement on legislation remaining to be introduced. I said I would do so on Thursday. On reflection it seemed to me to be preferable to give the statement today, in the light of the resolution which is now before us on the order paper. I believe, if the house has before it a statement of the business which remains to be disposed of, hon. members will be inclined to take a more favourable view of the resolution about To be proposed.

An act respecting article 41 of the charter of the united nations;
An act to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act;
A resolution respecting pensions or other superannuation benefits for senior appointees of the Department of External Affairs serving outside of Canada;
An act to vary the Saskatchewan natural resources agreement ;
An act to amend the National Housing Act, 1944;
An act to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939;

May I now reply specifically to the request made on Monday by the leader of the opposition for a statement of government legislation which remains to be introduced. All that I have mentioned so far has already appeared, or some notice of it has been given, in one or other of the publications of the house, but the following measures have still to be introduced -and may I say that most of them are prac-

tically ready now. There may be one or two that will be delayed before they are introduced, but I expect to see them on the order paper shortly.
First and foremost, there are the bills which arise out of the budget resolutions. They include:
A bill to amend the Excise Act.
A bill to amend the Income War Tax Act.
A bill to amend the Special War Revenue Act.
I understand that the number of these bills is about twelve in all. There are the following additional measures to be introduced by the Minister of Finance:

A bill to amend the Superannuation Act;
A bill respecting Canadian National Railways financing and guarantee;
A bill respecting Canadian National Railways refunding and financing;

A bill to amend the Insurance Act;

A bill to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act;

The following bills are to be introduced by other ministers:
A bill to amend the criminal code and possibly a separate bill to amend the criminal code respecting certain pari-mutuel charters;
A bill to amend the Identification of Criminals Act;
A bill to amend the Interpretation Act;
A bill to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act;
A bill respecting jurisdiction of United States service courts;
A bill respecting the dominion fuel board;
A bill to create a maritime commission;
A bill respecting the east slopes of the rockies;
A bill to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.
In addition to these measures, there are to be introduced the following resolutions:
A resolution approving the peace treaties with Italy, Hungary. Roumania and Finland;
A resolution approving the constitution of the international refugee organization;
A resolution approving the instrument of amendment of the constitution of the international labour organization;
A resolution respecting the conservation of fisheries on the high seas.

In addition to all this, I would say there remains such legislation as may grow out of the reports of the standing and special committees of the house. The latter include the committees on redistribution; the Dominion Elections Act; joint special committee on the Indian Act; committee on canteen funds; sessional committee on railways and shipping; committee on broadcasting.
I would remind the house that there is still before it a resolution to constitute a committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms, the debate on which is not yet concluded.
The debate on the budget has been in progress for some time past. It also is not yet concluded.

Finally, I must remind hon. members that all estimates of the present year remain to be passed, including those which have been before the house for some months, together with the usual supplementary estimates, also the appropriation bills to be based thereon.

As far as I am able to see at the moment, the statement I have made includes all the measures the government propose to introduce at the present session. 1 cannot guarantee that all will be proceeded with, nor can I guarantee that, as the session runs on, some matters may not arise which will require the introduction of additional measures. Of such at present I have no knowledge.

I must leave it to hon. members themselves whether they will not be prepared to endorse unanimously the motion I am about to bring before the house, which is to the effect that from next week on the-government is to take for its business the hour now reserved for private and public bills on Tuesdays and Fridays, also that the house is to sit on Wednesday evenings. Some understandings on some matters may have been reached with some hon. members by my colleagues the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As regards any such, I think we can find a way of meeting them in the course of the session. Near the end of the session there may be some private bills to which we shall have to give a night or two. I hope hon. members will see that here is a programme which, unless we are all prepared to expedite the business of the house, may carry us, not to the end of the summer but to the end of the year.

1469774,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.18.1.13,1947-05-21,unmatched,,,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,LEGISLATIVE PROGRAMME-PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS-WEDNESDAY EVENING SITTINGS,,I had an opportunity this morning of discussing this resolution with my colleagues, and they desire me to say that we are prepared to agree to the taking of the two evening hours, one on Tuesday and one on Friday, but we feel that the members still need Wednesday evening. My colleagues are not agreeable to taking that at the present time.

What has been said this afternoon by the Prime Minister about the very large amount of business yet to be done emphasizes again the desirability of doing something about the arrangement of the business of this house. It is obvious that we cannot proceed to do the business of parliament in the manner in which we have been accustomed to do it in bygone days. The British House of Commons, from which we take much of our procedure, owing to the pressure of business over the last number of years has had to devise ways and means of curtailing debate. We have tried to do that by agreement among the

parties, but we have failed. I know that on occasions I have given what amounted to a promise to other members of the house as to the number of speeches, and so on, but it is difficult to live up to any such undertaking. Something will have to be done about the rules.

In the interests of the health of the members of parliament we should not be sitting in this city all through the hot summer weather. Something needs to be done about the times of sitting of the house. Personally I favour the assembling of the house in the autumn for, say, six weeks, to get through the debate on the address, bring down some of the legislation, and try to conclude the business of the session by June 1. It is obvious that the days of three and four months sessions are gone, and something will have to be done to facilitate the business of the house and protect the health of the members. For several years past, members of the house have been unable to get away for a holiday and be with their families during a period when they can enjoy the sunshine. Judging from the long list of government business presented by the Prime Minister, if we deal with these matters properly we shall be here until September at the earliest. I wanted to place these views before the house in order that we may be thinking about them with a view to facilitating the business and protecting the health of hon. members.

1469775,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.18.1.14,1947-05-21,b11f5b30-7d32-44e6-b23c-a24561c1eaf5,ca.m.7719,Mr. MACKENZIE KING:,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,LEGISLATIVE PROGRAMME-PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS-WEDNESDAY EVENING SITTINGS,,I should like

to say a word in reply to my hon. friend. First of all, I wish to thank him and members of his group for agreeing to allowing the government to have the hour on Tuesday and Friday used for government business. I am afraid that I shall have to ask my hon. friend and his group to allow us to sit on Wednesday evenings. I would point out that it is easy to arrange the business of the house so that if, for example, on a Wednesday evening a number of members may wish to take the evening off, we can find some bills or estimates which all of us will agree are noncontroversial, and have them brought forward at that time. The British House of Commons has an enormous amount of business to transact and it manages to get through all its business with about one-third of the house present at any time of the day. I do not think that a member is called upon to be in his seat throughout all the time the house is sitting. If hon. members receive the bills in time to see what they contain, they can govern themselves accordingly. I believe that by arrangement between the leaders the programme can be made satisfactory.
Business of the House

With regard to the summer, I think that all of us would like to have some time off for a vacation, and perhaps none more than members of the government. I notice that often it is forgotten that, in addition to all the business of the House of Commons, members of the ministry have to carry on as well the business of government, whether the house is in session or not. It is a pretty heavy task, when the house is in session, to attend to correspondence, arrange for interviews, receive delegations, hold daily meetings of the cabinet, and consider the many matters that have to be discussed. I would draw attention to this fact, and it is one of the reasons why business is taking up so much time of parliaments today: there is a new class of public business altogether which has come to the fore since the war.

DIEFENBAKER (Lake Centre):,,EDIBLE OILS,ARRANGEMENT FOR SECURING ESSENTIAL SUPPLIES FROM ARGENTINA-NEWSPRINT SHIPMENTS,,I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance arising out of a statement appearing in the press today that a deal has been concluded between the government of Canada and the Peron government of the Argentine under which Canada will sell additional amounts of newsprint to the Argentine in exchange for vegetable oils from that country. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance):,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,EDIBLE OILS,ARRANGEMENT FOR SECURING ESSENTIAL SUPPLIES FROM ARGENTINA-NEWSPRINT SHIPMENTS,,An arrangement of the kind mentioned has been made. I had not thought I should take the time of the house to outline its terms, and I prepared a press release which is going out this afternoon, giving the particulars. However, my hon. friend and perhaps other members are interested, so I shall be very glad to give the house the details of the arrangement.

For some months we have been facing special difficulties in securing essential supplies of edible oils at reasonable prices. Since early in the war, as a result of a worldwide shortage, world supply and distribution of fats and oils have been the subject of discussion and allocations by international committees of which Canada has been a member, and under arrangements recently agreed upon we are entitled to import in 1947 about the same amounts as last year. However, that alone does not assure us supplies. Some of the sources from which we drew heavily last year are no longer available to us; and our need for imports is greater because domestic production of lard and other animal and marine oils and fats is running below last year's levels.

We have been confronted by a very difficult and serious situation. If certain negotiations had fallen through, we should have found ourselves lacking nearly half of our imports of edible oils. Moreover, since the larger part of our domestic supplies does not become available until later in the year, the full impact of this shortage would have fallen in the summer months. Less than half of normal supplies would have been available. Important industries would have been completely disorganized, particularly the baking industry. Shortening for household purposes would virtually have disappeared from retail stores.
Inquiries oj the Ministry

To meet this situation we have concluded arrangements which will go far toward assuring us of our minimum 1947 requirements of edible oils. The most important source of these oils available to us this year is the Argentine republic. We have therefore been negotiating with the government of that country to sell us up to 18,000 metric tons at prices which, while above last year's, are considerably below open market quotations prevailing at present, and in all the circumstances can be considered as not unreasonable. We have now reached a firm arrangement for 9,000 tons of oil, and negotiations covering a further 9,000 tons are well advanced.

In discussing these arrangements with us, the Argentine government has drawn our attention to the fact that they have been experiencing serious difficulties in securing their minimum supplies of newsprint and that their country is being less favoured in regard to supplies of newsprint from Canada than other countries also dependent on Canadian supplies. They were only prepared to make edible oils available to us under a special arrangement whereby newsprint tonnage would be made available to Argentina equivalent to the tonnage of oils received. Under this arrangement, which has been agreed to, if the full 18,000 tons of oil is received, the newsprint tonnage sent in return will be less than one-half of one per cent of total Canadian production, estimated at 4,350,000 tons for 1947. The arrangement will therefore have no significant effect on other shipments, domestic or export. If ordinary commercial newsprint shipments to Argentina continue, and I have no reason to believe they will not, the amount of Canadian newsprint going to that country will be somewhat greater than last year, but slightly below the 1940-45 average.

In order to avoid the complications involved in imposing export control, we are implementing our part of the bargain by instructing Canadian Commercial Corporation to buy newsprint from all the Canadian producers, in amounts depending on their production, and sell it to Argentina.

I have listened to the suggestion made with respect to the length of the sessions and the health of the members, and I feel it is an important one. While I sat here today I thought it would be a good idea to start in by ripping those awnings off the windows so as to let a little honest-to-God daylight into this impressive and depressing chamber. I am sure the architect who was responsible for this building must have placed the windows there for some purpose. There is no doubt that glass could be placed in them which would reflect light, and, on occasions, we could have the benefit of some daylight. The leader of the C.C.F. has said that we miss all the sunshine, and he is right.

This afternoon I am privileged to take part in an important debate. In doing so I feel I am favoured inasmuch as I did not lead off at the time when the presentation of the budget had had a certain stimulating effect-an effect, however, which died suddenly after the Canadian people had an opportunity to examine exactly what the budget meant.

It is customary, so it seems, to compliment the Minister of Finance, but I feel on this occasion I shall have to confine myself to complimenting him only upon his personality and his genial manner, because there is
The Budget-Mr. Case
nothing in the budget which merits compliment. I shall proceed in a moment or so to indicate why I take that view.

The minister presented to the house a budget in which he indicated a surplus of $352 million. It is only fair to say that he had no more to do with that surplus than did the man in the moon. The minister had only recently arrived from the Department of National Defence, and upon taking office in the Department of Finance he received a legacy, so to speak, from the sale of capital goods, the cost of which we have never been advised. Possibly more than $2 billion worth of goods, which Canadians bought through the purchase of victory bonds and through taxation, were sold for a total of $372 million. In spite of that enormous sum, the best the minister could indicate was a surplus of only $352 million. Yet it was so great that he himself did not know what to do with it. He proceeded to indicate a tapering off in the over-all amount of income tax, but in doing so he did not think of the little fellows who were earning a mere subsistence. He did not change the level at which the tax would apply.

This year he has budgeted for [DOT] a surplus, but with certain- qualifications. He has taken a rather gloomy attitude toward the future, and he is much in doubt as to his ability to deliver the goods. Because of the attitude of the Minister of Finance and the government generally there has been a failure to inspire business or to encourage private enterprise to play its full part, at a time when that inspiration and encouragement are so necessary in the affairs of this nation.

I feel that we might well weigh in the balance the experience of the minister's predecessor, who was charged with the responsibility of raising vast sums of money to carry this nation through a very trying period in our history. He proved himself equal to the task of extracting from the Canadian people, by taxation and by the sale of victory bonds -the best security in the world-at a time when patriotism was running at great heat, untold billions of dollars. But with his mind fixed upon such a large target he failed to weigh in the balance the capabilities of the Canadian people in time of peace and so we found in the estimates last year that the former minister of finance, backed by his years of experience, budgeted for a deficit of approximately $300 million.
When the present Minister of Finance appeared before the House of Commons he gallantly pointed out that through the good management of his predecessor he was able

to present a surplus of $352 million. I wonder if the Canadian people realize that they were just about $700 million out in their estimates. In other words, it was nothing more or less than a pure guess. A school boy could have come just about as close to it. If the present Minister of Finance with his limited experience can budget more accurately, then there is no reason to believe that the administration needs any particular financial talent to administer the affairs of the Department of Finance. I say that we must wait and see. I think the Minister of Finance would have shown greater courage and would have inspired the people of Canada had he copied the example of his predecessor and budgeted this year for a. deficit of a quarter of a billion dollars, cut right across the levels of taxation and unshackled the restrictions which are handicapping this nation as it fights its way to greater heights in peace time.

I should like to refer to the way in which the budget has been accepted. During the war I remember listening to a talented lady address a public meeting. She said, ""If you want to know how the war is going, do not read the headlines, just look at the financial sheet."" If you want to know how much this government has inspired business in this country, just turn to the financial sheet in your daily newspaper and there you will find a shrinkage in values to the extent of millions upon millions of dollars.

I am saying this with all kindness and respect, because in making my criticism I want it thoroughly understood that I bear no personal ill will toward any of those sitting opposite. I appreciate indeed the responsibilities which they have assumed, but at the same time as a member sitting on this side of the house I can afford to be critical of their methods. This government has carried on government at the administrative level, but I challenge any member of the government to stand up and say that they have solved one major national problem since the closing days of the war.

I wish to deal now with what I consider to be the national problems facing this country, and then I shall assess the value the government places upon the manner in which it has solved these problems. For instance, I am going to ask: Does the government believe that it has solved the housing problem? My experience is that there are scores upon scores of people who are still seeking shelter. There are thousands who believe that government policy has been such as to hamper the construction industry, and that the restrictions which have been retained have handicapped the manufacturers and suppliers.

A resolution was passed by the council of my home city and addressed to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). The clerk of the municipality has communicated the resolution in the following terms: As a result of requests received from the Owen Sound rehabilitation council and from various citizens, the city council has instructed me by resolution, passed unanimously at its meeting held May 12, 1947, to write you requesting that controls upon building materials for the Owen Sound area be removed in order that the same may be released to individuals desiring to undertake the construction of their own homes and to complete homes upon which construction has been started and cannot be completed owing to inability to obtain necessary materials.

I think I should point out in this connection that in the past eighteen months, the municipal corporation has sold to individuals, 187 building lots upon the condition that the purchasers thereof will construct a dwelling before obtaining title thereto. None of these purchasers to date, has been able to complete his dwelling and claim his deed, due to the fact, in almost every ease, that building materials cannot be secured by individuals who have no priority.

The local government bodies are charged with the responsibility of finding some means by which they can provide shelter for their people. Their appeal to the government is to get the building industry out of the muddling mess they have been put into, and give private enterprise a chance to show its worth.

I ask the government: Has it solved the problem of production? Goods are in short supply. Almost any article of great necessity is difficult to obtain. I have heard hon. members claim that they are unable to secure even a shirt, but I believe that that situation has improved somewhat. But the government has failed to solve the problem of supply or production.

I ask further: Has the government solved the agricultural problem? All I have to do is to point to the thousands upon thousands of vacant farms throughout Canada to show whether farming has lost its attractiveness, or whether the government has inspired people to return to the soil and dig from the good earth the wealth the nation depends upon, the food that the world is seeking to prevent starvation. It is true that many factors enter into this question. Farming has not lost all its attractiveness, and I would be the first to encourage a return to the farm lands of this country. I believe there is something in store for our farmers, but the tendency is to make it so attractive for people to leave the farms and seek to earn their living in urban centres, in the bright lights, that it is almost impossible for farmers to carry on and secure the help they need for their farms. Indeed the farmer cannot depend upon a thirty-six hour, a forty hour or a forty-four hour week or an eight hour day. His time is set by the sun, and he must employ his labour and talents from daylight to darkness in order that his work can be completed. However, we find the natural tendency is to encourage people to become more or less dependent upon some central authority. In other words we are developing amongst our people a nation of leaners rather than leaders. The natural trend is toward governmental paternalism. In time, then we look back and assess this period in our day and generation, we shall find that it was one of the most dangerous periods through which we have passed.

History, Mr. Speaker, has a habit of repeating itself. Students of history will tell you that when the great Roman empire was on the-march, when they were beating their ploughshares into swords, they were masters and monarchs of all they surveyed; but the moment they began to make it more attractive for people to live in the urban centres, when their people began to flock into their towns and cities from the great agricultural lands, the great nation began to crumble and decay, and today not a vestige of that empire remains. As a matter of fact we hear no more of the great Roman empire.

I can think of the days gone by in the history of the country, when it was determined that we should become a confederation, when there gathered first at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and later in the city of Quebec, those who later were known as the fathers of confederation. I am sure the Minister of Finance and his advisers must be greatly concerned about the constant draining off of United States dollars or United States exchange at a time when we need that exchange to carry on our business. I could not understand why the exchange situation was levelled at parity, and I asked the then minister of finance, now [DOT] the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) where the pressure came from. Do hon. members ever stop to realize the advantage that we enjoyed? Yet the Minister of Finance referred to this in his budget address and said that on the

whole it was working out satisfactorily, or words to that effect. Do hon. members ever stop to think that this is a time when we are seeking to expand Canadian markets? After all, gold remains a standard of value because it is durable, and we have plenty of it in our hinterland and in our rocks, but we must encourage miners and free enterprise to take this precious metal and put it where it can be used in a monetary sense as a backlog for the nation's trading balances.

I think it was the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) who made the remark that the best thing that could happen to Canada would be for the United States to raise the price of gold. I regret that we take that attitude, because this is one instance in which Canada can indeed offer to give a sense of leadership. We should not have to wait for the United States to increase the value of gold. For our own protection and for the benefit of one of our great natural resources, one of the largest employers of labour, we should set our course to encourage the mining of gold. It would be within the realm of possibility to pay $40 an ounce, for native-mined gold, or even more; because once you have paid $40 an ounce for gold you are no longer paying interest upon that sum; you have a durable medium of exchange which will satisfy all trading balances throughout the civilized and trading world.

medicine, law, or any other recognized profession, in order that such parents might be encouraged to divert some of their money towards that purpose. I for one know something about the sacrifices generally that are made in that respect.

I have said that there has been no leadership. There is no overall planning. There is no programme of expansion or building, and we know that our country is languishing from lack of direction.

I look upon our municipal councils as the very bulwark of democracy. They live close to the people and can interpret the people's needs and wishes better than any other level of government. We know that services are badly needed. Take, for instance, our educational institutions. Thousands upon thousands of dollars must be spent, and spent immediately; and certainly over a period of years hundreds of millions will be spent to guarantee to our children a proper education. Would members of the House of Commons be surprised to learn that in Saskatchewan alone almost one thousand Indian children are being denied education because there are no schools? If you think I am wrong about that, I want to read into the record a state-

ment by one whom I consider sufficient authority to back me up on this issue. I quote as follows:

1469857,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.20,1947-05-21,135d802e-28f0-4d51-bbb7-24d5271e5abd,ca.m.2601,Mr. RONALD MOORE (Churchill):,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, more than sufficient time has elapsed to permit the country at large to digest the sensational sections of the budget. The result, it would appear from information at hand, is such that, instead of finding himself or herself with a potentially greater income, the man or woman with an average pay cheque or envelope finds the opposite to be the case. In fact, the months of May and' June will see them further behind, financially speaking.

On numerous occasions the attention of the house has been directed to the tables illustrating the ""percentage reduction from present rates"" of income tax to that of the proposed rates of income tax. When one looks at the tables in question it cannot be denied that it is correct that the government can save the taxpayer a sum of money ranging from fifty-four per cent in the lower brackets to seven per cent in the upper brackets over the amount contributed currently. However, an examination of another set of government statistics, appearing in the same document with the tables of reductions, reveals that ""the cost of living and wholesale price index"" has steadily risen in the instance of all items from 124 in June, 1946, to 127 in December, 1946, to 128 in February of this year. These figures are taken from the budget in Hansard of Tuesday, April 29, 1947, and can be seen on page 2600 of that document. The same table gives a more dreary picture in the instance of ""wholesale prices"", which reveal a figure of 142 for June, 1946; 145 for December, 1946; 148 for January, 1947, and 153 for February, 1947.

It would be most enlightening to know whar the price index reveals for the current month, now that prices are really starting to climb, with the lifting of subsidies and price ceilings on a long line of goods.
The Budget-Mr. Moore

Allow me to illustrate in another fashion what I have just noted. It is found that in the ease of a married man with two children of family allowance age the government will save this man with an SI,800 annual income the truly stupendous sum of $16 in his next income tax return. That is about thirty cents a week. If this typical family uses only three pounds of butter a week the saving in income tax is completely wiped out by the action of the government in removing the subsidy on butter. Add to this the rising cost of eggs, Cheddar cheese and other staples of the dinner table, and the so-called saving in income tax gradually mounts to a sizable deficit. The humotous side, if such it can be called in dealing with a serious subject of this kind, is that today the family in question is also paying more money in higher prices, whereas the so-called saving in income tax, running as high as fifty-four per cent, does not take effect until July 1 of this year.

I should like to deal for a few moments with the basis on which the reductions in income tax have been computed in the present budget. The Minister of Finance has said that the reductions are as high as fifty-four per cent in the lower brackets, and as low as six and seven per cent in the higher brackets. As we check the figures in the budget there can be no doubt that this is true; but one thing has bothered me. I wonder why the income tax reductions this year have been computed on a percentage basis. People who have made a study of previous budgets introduced in this house tell me that reductions have always been computed on a dollar basis. If the amount to be contributed in income tax were either increased or decreased in any previous budget, the differences were given on a dollar basis. Of course it is quite easy to convert the percentage basis to the dollar basis, and in order to develop the argument I wish to present this afternoon I am going to do that at the present time.

Let us take, for example, the fifty-four per cent reduction in income tax paid by those coming within the lower income brackets. For a single person earning $800 per annum, this reduction of fifty-four per cent means a saving of $6 in the amount of money he will contribute to the federal treasury this year. Last year he had to pay $11, so that the saving is fifty-four per cent; but the dollar saving is only $6 per annum. Take the case of a married man with no children, whose annual income is $1,800. He, too, saves fifty-four per cent. This year the new income tax rates will save him $16, while on the basis of a full twelve months' period the dollar saving 83166-211J

will be $32. Let us consider for a moment the man who receives a much larger income and who has been given a reduction of only seven per cent. According to the tables, the income tax reduction of seven per cent applies to incomes of around $200,000 or more. Of course such incomes will be made up of salaries, investments and so on; but the seven per cent reduction on $200,000 amounts to $10,385 per annum. Then take the case of a man receiving an annual salary of $5,000. His reduction in income tax is fourteen times greater than the reduction given the man in the $1,000 a year bracket. Similarly the reduction given the man earning $10,000 per annum; his reduction in income tax is almost thirty times greater than the reduction of the man earning $1,000 a year.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Thomas John Bentley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4983dfa5-ae0c-4441-a68b-5fa6c9bd729f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1469862,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.25,1947-05-21,135d802e-28f0-4d51-bbb7-24d5271e5abd,ca.m.2601,Mr. MOORE:,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,I appreciate the hon. member's question, since I endeavour to study these questions as deeply as possible. The point I am making is that I believe the government should1 have completely eliminated the income tax on all incomes within the lower brackets. During the past two years the trades and labour council and the Canadian Congress of Labour have submitted briefs asking that all incomes within the lower brackets, that is up to $2,000 for a married person and $1,000 for a single person, should be absolved from the payment of income tax. I think a careful study of the budget indicates that this could be done and the government could still maintain sufficient revenue adequately to carry on the services of the country. As we peruse the pages of the present budget we find that the reduction in personal income taxes amounts to around $70,000,000 a year, while the reduction in the excess profits tax amounts to $269,000,000, or approximately four times as much. The taxation statistics put out by the Department of National Revenue for 1946 show the amount collected in taxation from the income group I have been discussing, that is those receiving from $1,000 to $2,000 per annum,
The Budget-Mr. Moore

in round figures amounts to approximately $145,000,000. So I submit that if the government had wished to do so they could have largely eliminated taxation in this field and made up the difference by way of extractions from the excess profits tax.

I do not want any hon. member to think I have anything against companies and corporations in Canada which are making profits, but I think the excess profits tax is a fair tax because it is based upon profits which are greater than normal. During the depression years from 1936 to 1939 we found that a large number of Canadian companies were able to make pretty fair profits. When the war broke out, the excess profits taxation was imposed, under which the average profit for the four years mentioned was known as the standard profit. Anything in excess of that became excess profits and subject to heavy taxation. I believe the government should continue that plan into the peacetime era. I believe it should be continued for this reason, that in Canada today we have a twenty-seven year backlog of production. First, we had the depression, during which a considerable backlog of production developed. Then, we had the war period, when another backlog of production developed. We also have foreign markets, and at the present time our industries are running all-out in an effort to supply them. So today the profits of Canadian industry are the highest in the history of this country, and I think the government should take steps to collect a large proportion of that money in taxation, which could be used to provide better social services to our people.

,Progressive Conservative,,Harry Rutherford Jackman,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5f9946d8-6285-42b5-8cf0-d207fcf461a7&Language=E&Section=ALL
1469864,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.27,1947-05-21,135d802e-28f0-4d51-bbb7-24d5271e5abd,ca.m.2601,Mr. MOORE:,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,I take it, Mr. Speaker, that companies and corporations are very much like individuals. There may be two individuals in a certain line of business. One will make a success; the other will not be able to get along so well. I believe a case such as that mentioned by the hon. member should be considered by the government, and if it is found necessary to make reductions in such a case, then I believe those reductions should be made so that the taxes on those industries which are not as successful would be

lower. However I do not see that this argument has very much weight at the present time. There may be some industries in regard to which certain reservations would have to be made; but, generally speaking, Canadian industry is running all-out today and making greater profits than ever before. I have in my hand a number of press clippings: ""B.C. Pulp and Paper doubles its profit this year. Nets $991,000."" Another, ""Borden's Milk sales the highest in four years."" Another article is headed ""76 per cent profit gain for oil company""-and this is the Canadian Oil Companies Limited. Another states ""Sears, Roebuck doubled"" its profit, and another states, ""Price's net profit shows 123 per cent boost.""

Those are things which I think the government should cash in on. It should use the excess profits tax to the full, and collect taxes in order to provide social services for this country. No one believes more fully than I do in the services rendered by the federal government, but I think it is following a wrong policy in not fully taxing big business in Canada. There are other advantages which would occur if the suggestion were followed that taxation on smaller incomes be wiped out. One would be a tremendous saving in the labour of administration which goes into the work of compiling, printing and checking income tax papers of the groups which should not be paying taxes on small earnings. This saving in work would then permit the harassed revenue department to concentrate still more on larger incomes, which would result in still greater revenues for the government in tracking down those who are not now paying the income tax they should be paying.

It is true that this is another problem. Yet it is a fact that the removal of income tax from the lower levels would permit revenue officials to concentrate more on those who -are avoiding their responsibility by not paying their full share of income tax. This does not mean that the great bulk of income tax returns are incorrect, because it is felt that the great majority of people are inherently honest. However, among those in the higher brackets there is a fair percentage who are not paying all that the tax laws require. It is this group which I have in mind, and which revenue officials will admit exists in goodly numbers.

Whilst I am on this subject of taxing still further the higher income tax payers, I might observe that action should have been taken in absolving from taxation the incomes of married women who are working and earning sums less than $1,000. It has been the experi-
The Budget-Mr. Moore
ence of many that married women who go out and earn some money in addition to that earned by their husbands, usually do so because there is an economic need for such earnings.

I do not believe the average husband desires that his wife should be a bread-winner. But if it is necessary, in these days of high living costs, for both to earn a livelihood, then some assistance should be given these people by lowering the amounts they should pay in income tax to the federal treasury.

I cannot help coming to the conclusion that a reduction of the amounts to be collected in income tax in the near future has resulted in no benefits such as the government attempted to visualize in the budget now under discussion. I do not wish to say more at this time with respect to the personal income tax.

I now turn to the excess profits tax. I am of the opinion that a most serious error has been made by the government in reducing its income from this source. Since the name implies that these are ""excess profits"", there should have been no argument whatsoever as to the reduction or otherwise of this tax. Apparently, according to the government, it is perfectly satisfactory for large business organizations and individuals not to be taxed as heavily on their more-than-normal profits.

,Liberal,,Douglas Charles Abbott,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1469868,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.31,1947-05-21,135d802e-28f0-4d51-bbb7-24d5271e5abd,ca.m.2601,Mr. MOORE:,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,According to the figures in the budget, the revenue from the excess profits tax will mean that the federal treasury stands to gain approximately $500 million. It is possible that the saving granted to large business groups in respect of their excess profits tax will be more than sufficient to meet the federal government's obligations in respect of old age pensions payments. I could go through the budget and show other instances where the amount saved by business in reduced excess profits taxes would pay for the cost of other essential services. And hon. members should note with care that these are excess profits.
I cannot by any stretch of the imagination worry myself about the so-called burden

carried by big business when called upon to pay the treasury taxes on their excess profits. After all, this is not a matter of paying taxes on ordinary profits. Again I emphasize that these are taxes on excess profits. According to the income tax laws, there is more than enough leeway for these large corporations to meet many obligations, which can include large amounts of money for all sorts of expenses, depreciation, sinking funds, and a great host of other items which are properly deductible under the law from excess profits. With these facts in mind, it can scarcely be said that the keeping of the excess profits tax at its former level 'would be a hardship on big business.

The government is considering amending the statute which deals with the excess profits tax. If this change is to be implemented, plans should be made to retain that objective whereby taxes on excess profits would continue to remain at a high level so as to ensure the government a large source of income and at the same time permit further tax reductions in the salaries of those in the lowest income brackets.

A study of the revenues the government expects from the huge taxes on items such as candy, soft drinks, chewing gum and other similar items reveals that these revenues are not so great when compared with total revenues expected. It is granted that the figures will reach a sum of about $32 million, most of which will be taken from the small allowances of young children, and from poor people, who indulge in consuming these penny products.

To make up for this loss of revenue, if these so-called nuisance taxes were either wiped out or reduced considerably, the taxes on such items as pari-mutuel bets, luxury products which only the wealthy can afford, might well be raised to meet the difference. Beyond question, the revenues received from parimutuel bets should be much higher than they are at the present time, on the principle that if people have money to throw away at race tracks the government should take advantage of this tendency and collect every possible cent. As the racing business is conducted today, most of the money does not go to the betting fans but rather into the coffers of the operators. I would much rather deprive race track operators of some of their dollars than increase the cost of a chocolate bar for a child. As the situation stands today, that is what is taking place.
One of the items which contributes to the aigh cost of living is the sales tax which, in my view, in many ways could be described as one of the nuisance taxes. Since there are
The Budget-Mr. Moore

few items not subject to sales tax, a reduction of one or two per cent in this tax would reduce the cost of living by an almost similar amount. This is a subject the government might well consider, and thus give some reduction in the cost of living.

I am sure most hon. members have within the past four or five months received letters and resolutions requesting increased pensions for blind persons. Any move on the part of the government to increase these allowances to blind people would be a worthy gesture.

I should like to devote the time remaining at my disposal to a discussion of matters affecting my own constituency. I come from a part of the country which is comparatively new so far as development is concerned. The matter with which I should like to deal now has been brought to the attention of this house already by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller). 1469871,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.34,1947-05-21,d5718e82-6d02-4656-8d03-bb9f9b5d5c86,ca.m.8420,Mr. J. I. HAMEL (St. Maurice-Lafleche):,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with my remarks on the budget in my own language, I think this would be a proper time to congratulate my English-speaking colleagues who have used the French language in part of their speeches. To my mind they were well advised in doing so, because they showed to the

people of this country their desire for a better understanding between our people. My remarks will deal, first, with the budget and then, second, with federal-provincial relations.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the budget. I do not intend to play the financial expert, but simply to discuss this document as would the average citizen, who will be called upon to pay the costs.

Most newspapers have given a lot of publicity to the reductions announced in the speech of the Hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), whom I am pleased to congratulate for the extraordinary ability he showed in defending what, in my opinion, was a bad cause.
The budget introduced on April 29 last, is bad because it is antisocial and prejudicial to the family, for the following reasons:

First, indirect taxation remains at the same level and, according to forecasts, will produce $300,000,000 more than last year. One does not have to be a financial expert to realize to what extent indirect taxation, added to the price paid by the consumer, increases the cost of living.

Second, the reductions announced in the income tax are absolutely misleading. When they are considered in relation with the general economic policy of the government and the country, it becomes plain that wage-earners in the lower brackets will be more heavily burdened in 1947 and 1948 than last year.

A few figures will suffice, I believe, to prove that statement. Take the single man earning $750 a year. He will be entitled to a reduction of $6 on his income tax; on the other hand, due to the cancellation of subsidies which he previously enjoyed on certain goods, due to the increased prices of certain essential commodities, he will be more heavily burdened than last year.

Supposing that he consumed one pint of milk every day, or 183 quarts per year, he will have to pay $5.49 more on account of the removal of the milk subsidy. If he pays $12 per month for his room, the rental increase will mean for him the payment of $14.40 more during the year. Supposing, further, that he consumes one pound of butter per week, he will have to pay, under that item, $5.20 more. I could keep on adding to that list. In fact, he pays $6 less for income tax, but for three essential commodities he will have to pay $25.09 more. Can any one advance seriously the claim that the position of people in the lower salary brackets is being improved?

Those facts are all the more striking when the position of family heads is considered. Let us take the case of a married man with no children whose yearly income is $1,600. The tax reduction from which he will benefit will amount to $12. He will have to pay $10.95 more for his milk. If his rental was $20 per month, he will have to add $24 a year on account of the 10 per cent increase, and probably $7.50 to cover the rise in the price of butter. The net result is a decrease of $12 in his income tax and an increase of $42.45 in the cost of living, hence a net decrease of $30.45 in his purchasing power merely for those items.

The position of the married man with two children is still worse. If his income amounts to $1,800 the tax reduction in his case is $10. He will have to pay $21.90 more for his milk on the basis of two quarts per day. For his rent, supposing he pays $25 per month, he will have to pay $30 more for the full year. As regards butter, the extra expenditure will be $10.40, if his family's consumption is two pounds per week. The net result is a reduction of $10 in his income tax and an increase of $62.30 in the cost of living; hence a net decrease of $52.30 in his purchasing power.

Such a state of things will, to my mind, give rise to labour conflicts which are always very unfortunate for the people as the whole. In order that the working masses might be provided with a suitable purchasing power, all wage-earners, and married persons more particularly, whose income did not exceed $3,000 should pay no income tax.

To prevent our middle class-for which I have a great deal of sympathy-from being taxed too heavily as a result of the exemptions granted small wage-earners, the government should resort to radical means and bring about a monetary reform in order to reduce the budget by some $450,000,000, which amount only represents the interest we must pay.

profits, he will wonder whether at present, when companies are accumulating profits that are perhaps unequalled in history, it is fitting to eliminate taxes on excess profits.

Income tax levied on corporations, dividends and interest increased from 95 millions in 1939 to approximately 303-5 millions in 1945, representing an increase of slightly over 300 per cent.
On the other hand, as happens in practically every war, income derived from capital increased far more than that derived from labour.

Again, at page 908 of the ""Canada Year Book"" for the year 1946, I find that income derived from labour increased from $2,540,000,000 in 1939 to $5,037,000,000 in 1945, while income derived from investments increased from $782,000,000 in 1939 to $1,811,000,000 in 1945.

I repeat that, in my humble opinion, such an attitude will give rise to industrial disputes for which the greater responsibility will fall upon the government. In order to ensure ""ocial peace and the normal distribution of production which can be derived from our economic organization, it would be but fair and just to decrease the return on capital and increase the return on labour; but we are I Mr. Hamel.]
doing exactly the opposite. No wonder that subversive theories find suitable ground in our country.

The Budget-Mr. Hamel
remission to Great Britain of an incalculable debt and, finally, the billion and a quarter loan to the United Kingdom.

In view of the difference between the preliminary and final proposals, there is doubt as to whether the real intention, the real object of the central power is not, first and foremost, that of interfering with provincial jurisdictions, of controlling the expenditures of the provinces, in short, of placing them under trusteeship.

Ambiguity as to the objects; ambiguity as to the real meaning of the proposals; ambiguity as to the real motives behind the proposed agreements; ambiguity as to their duration; ambiguities resulting from separate agreements; ambiguities in the statement of the Minister of Finance, as appearing in his press release of January 25, 1947.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a supporter of the Union Nationale, but I cannot refrain from commending the stand taken by the premier of the province of Quebec, when he refused to jeopardize, on the strength of such ambiguities, the provincial legislative autonomy in such an important section of the fiscal field.

From the sad experience of the past and particularly from our more recent experience of the thirties, we should be desperately blind if we did not now take the necessary steps to adopt measures in order to protect the Canadian population, as I have just said in French, against the calamity of another economic crisis, which, according to the trend of the past and under the conditions which have prevailed so far, is due for 1949 or 1950. Therefore it is the duty of this government and our first duty as members of this parliament to see to it that the Canadian people of all regions and all classes, the Canadian people whom we represent in this house, do not experience once again at least in our lifetime the social injustices, the sufferings and the iniquities which will be brought about by another, the fifteenth, economic crisis.

In a country as great as Canada, so immensely rich in lands, forests, fisheries, minerals and other natural resources, with a small population of not quite 13,000,000 inhabitants, we do not want, as was suggested by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche, to go back to the conditions which prevailed in 1921, for example, or in 1930, or even to the conditions which prevailed from 1937 to 1939, because, if we remember well, the last economic crisis was sunk in the rivers of blood of the last great war. We do not want to see again in this country thousands of Canadians on direct relief, or living in a state next to starvation merely because of the lack of proper provision in the constitution of this country, or the lack of collaboration between federal and provincial powers, or, in other words, because of the blindness, the short-sightedness and the foolishness of men.

If peace is to guarantee anything to the Canadian citizen it must at least guarantee full employment, just compensation for employment, and the establishment of a liberty of enterprise truly and positively democratic. The sort of economy we have
The Budget-Mr. Arsenault

experienced in the past, particularly from 1918 to 1939, between the two world wars, cannot guarantee either full employment, just compensation for a good day's work, or the establishment of a truly democratic liberty of enterprise. I for one would hate to think that future conditions of employment in this country could be, as has been the case in the past, solely determined by the private judgment, good or bad, of individuals, ignorant or speculative or selfish or short-sighted, who. within less than twenty-five years, have led the Canadian population to the graveyards of two major economic crises.

That is to say, Mr. Speaker, that, from now on, economic forces will have to be curbed or guided in this country. From now on, if we want to avoid the tragic consequences of another economic depression the responsi-oility for full employment in Canada must rest upon the federal government. We cannot go back to the past. We are headed for the future; and in the future this Canadian government will have as its first duty to exercise a guiding influence on the propensity of the Canadian people to consume; for example, partly through the government's scheme of taxation, partly by influencing rates of interest or promoting investments, and partly by other devices such as developing Canada's international trade, for example, and so forth. Whether we like it or not, this means that we have now reached the point in our economy where, in these ever-changing world conditions, this country needs a certain amount of planned economy; that we have reached a point where the devices necessary to ensure full employment will involve a larger extension of the traditional functions of the federal government.

Under the worn-out system of laissez-faire, no means is open to the federal government of this country to rectify economic distress except through competitive struggles for outside markets. We have now to learn-and this is important, because this is where wars come from-how to provide permanent prosperity and full employment in this country by applying adequate and proper adjustments to our domestic policy. International trade should cease to be what it has been in the past, a desperate expedient to maintain employment at home by forcing sales on foreign markets, by merely shifting our unemployment problems to other countries. This government, conscious of its responsibility toward the Canadian people and strong in the experience of the past, is seeking the best possible devices in order to achieve that end of attaining full employment and assuring the progress and prosperity of this country.

In so far as the prevention of economic depressions is concerned, we cannot but readily admit that the federal government has grave responsibilities. And in order that this government may stabilize-and I should like the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche to listen to this carefully-the volume of employment in Canada in such a way as to prevent another economic crisis, it is essential that our fiscal policy be perfectly harmonized with our international trade policy, with our tariff policy and with our monetary policy, all four of which fall under federal jurisdiction.

In making its proposals to the provinces, the federal government has clearly expressed its views on how the objectives set forth can be attained. Its view may be summarized briefly by quoting four paragraphs from page 7 of the federal proposals of August, 1945. They are:
First, to facilitate private enterprise to produce and provide employment.
Secondly, to promote bold action by the state in those fields in which the public interest calls for public enterprise in national development.
Thirdly, to provide through public investment, productive employment for our human and physical resources when international and other conditions adversely affect employment.
Fourthly, to provide on the basis of small regular payments against large and uncertain individual risks for such hazards and disabilities as unemployment, sickness and old age.

However, it is a fact that section 91, subsection 3, of the British North America Act gives the Canadian parliament the power of raising of money by any mode or S3rstem of taxation. That means direct as well as indirect taxation. This power has been confirmed over and over again by the judicial committee of the privy council. For instance, a decision of the judicial committee in 1932 in Silver Brothers versus the Attorney General for Quebec and the Attorney General for Canada reads:

The two taxations, dominion and provincial, can stand side by side without interfering with each other, *but as soon as you come to the concomitant privilege of absolute priority they cannot stand side by side and must clash; consequently the dominion must prevail.
In connection with the federal right to direct taxation, there is another decision of the judicial committee in 1924 in Caron versus The King, whieh reads:
The dominion income tax is intra vires of the dominion parliament, and its application to the salaries of a provincial government minister is valid.
The last decision I should like to quote is one given in 1937 in Forbes versus the Attorney General for Manitoba, which reads:

Lastly, there is here no conflict between the dominion and provincial income tax legislation. Both income tax may co-exist and be enforced without clashing, and theTe is no room for the application of the doctrine of the occupied field.

In view of the very text of our constitution and the many decisions of the judicial committee granting the Canadian parliament unlimited power in the matter of direct as well as indirect taxation, how can this government be accused of wanting to reach some agreement '""ith the provinces for the sole purpose of securing new fields of taxation when it is so clearly established that the Canadian parliament has already both fields of taxation, direct as well as indirect, at its unlimited disposal.

1469932,ca.proc.d.1947-05-21.26.1.95,1947-05-21,414611c5-593a-4084-9c41-ea6d6a98f438,ca.m.8762,Mr. ARSENAULT:,,THE BUDGET,DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Where and how do the federal proposals infringe on provincial autonomy? There have been repeated demands for a new conference with the provinces following the failure of so many dominion-provincial conferences. The hon. member for St. Mauriee-Lafleche claims that a separate arrangement between the federal government and an individual province is following an unjust practice. If the autonomy of any province is to be respected, then a conference of the provinces would have no power over that individual province.

Seven provinces have now accepted the federal government proposals in order to avoid double taxation. No new conference of the provinces could make those seven provinces give up their agreements with the Canadian government. No new conference of provinces could force the remaining two provinces to enter into a financial arrangement with the federal government if they do not want to. The idea of renting by one government of fields of taxation to another government is a tragic admission of a serious weakness in our constitution, but a dominion-provincial conference would have no power to amend the constitution, no more than it has the power to dictate the course that any individual province should follow.

However, there should be a permanent division of the direct taxation field between the federal government and the provinces. In order to achieve that objective, there would have to be an amendment to the constitution in connection with the division of fiscal powers. It is obvious that certain of the direct taxation powers should be assigned exclusively to the provinces, but this has not as yet been done, either by the text of the constitution, or by the decisions of the judicial committee.

The amendment of our constitution should not be long delayed, unless the Canadian government reaches a satisfactory basis of cooperation with all the provinces. The risk of another economic depression and of communism is too great in this country for us to lose any more time arguing over such an important issue.

Time is for action, and I do not see that we have too much time ahead of us. I suggest that the whole question of federal-provincial relations should now soon be referred to the people of Canada as the main issue to be settled at the earliest possible day by way of a general election; and wishing that for the good of this country we some day in Canada benefit by perfect harmony between the federal and provincial powers, may I be permitted, before resuming my seat, to quote two paragraphs from page 408 of ""Problems of Canadian Sovereignty"", by Doctor Maurice Ollivier:

Two classes of people have been the enemies of Canadian unity; those who have placed another country above Canada in their love, affection and admiration, ever stressing the alleged superiority of that country over our own, and secondly, those nationalists with a narrow provincial concept who have constantly attacked the federal power just as if .the provinces were not represented at Ottawa and were not part of the federal system but separate entities fighting a foreign government.
They have wilfully confused provincial rights with minority rights and constantly refused to acknowledge that what benefited one province *was for the advantage of the other.

Canada as a whole cannot be happy and prosperous when one part suffers from poverty, sickness, deplorable living conditions or drought whether these be the result of low wages, bad housing or an act of God.

We should, therefore, bend our efforts to maintain in this country popular government, individual liberty and social justice as the only means capable of assuring to all an equal chance to work and to profit from the better life that comes with material progress, in other words, of guaranteeing to all, freedom from want and freedom from fear, remembering that economic and political nationalism has always, in the past, created racial strife and world disasters.
